paras: The lynching of Judy Metts was the hanging of a Black woman by a party of disguised horsemen near Martin's Depot, Laurens County, South Carolina, on the night of April 9, 1881, after they took her from a constable who had arrested her for barn-burning. A coroner's jury found that she died at the hands of persons unknown, and Governor Hagood later offered $200 for each of the lynchers. Because the charge was arson rather than rape or murder, and the victim a woman, much of the South Carolina press condemned the lynching as murder.

On the night of Sunday, April 3, a barn belonging to J. S. Blalock at Martin's Depot was set on fire and burned, and its closeness to the house led to the belief that the dwelling had also been the target. Blalock concluded that the fire had been set by Judy Metts, a woman living on his plantation, who had been accused two years earlier of burning a Mr. Simpson's dwelling but never tried. On Saturday, April 9, he swore out a warrant before Trial Justice N. S. Harris at Clinton, who gave it to Constable Samuel Gary.

Gary arrested her on Blalock's plantation and started with her for Clinton about 8 o'clock that night, though the News and Courier dispatch put the arrest at about 5 o'clock. About two miles above Martin's Depot, nearly opposite Henry M. Hunter's residence, a party of men on horseback, their faces covered with cloth with eyeholes, overtook them. Some of the men carried off the constable and others the woman; by his own statement Gary was held about an hour and told to "git," and he went on to Clinton.

The next morning she was found dead, hanging by the neck from a tree about twenty feet up and about 200 yards from the road. She was cut down on Sunday, and on Monday a coroner's jury returned a verdict of death by hanging at the hands of persons unknown. Black residents buried her the same day; the Newberry Herald gave her age as about thirty-five and said she left a husband and children.

Through late April the papers reported that no one had been arrested and no steps taken to find the lynchers. The Rev. A. C. Legette of Laurens wrote to the Laurensville Herald that the colored people were "much excited and incensed," and that the constable should explain the night arrest and prove he was not an accomplice. By early May Governor Hagood had offered $200 apiece for the arrest and conviction of the lynchers, whom the Anderson Intelligencer put at some twenty-five and the Lancaster Ledger at thirty. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and the Newberry Herald's chronology of 1881 listed the case only as a lynching for house-burning.

The first reports were short South Carolina items saying a woman had been lynched for trying to burn Blalock's premises, and the Newberry Herald at once judged the hanging "neither excusable nor justifiable." A fuller News and Courier dispatch then ran in the Richmond Dispatch and the Chicago Tribune, and shorter versions reached Ohio, Missouri and Indiana, where one paper named the victim "Ann Cowan" and placed the lynching at “Spartansburg”.

Within South Carolina the News and Courier called the lynching "murder," arguing that arson was already a capital crime the courts would punish. The Anderson Intelligencer, the Keowee Courier and the Pickens Sentinel condemned it too, while holding that lynching could be excused for rape or murder. The Abbeville Press and Banner went further, attacking what it called the state's "habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes," saying the constable should be held to account, and mocking the apologists for lynching.

Its stand drew a rebuke from the Pickens Sentinel, which feared it would hand Northern Republicans ammunition, and support from the Georgetown Times. In Washington the National Republican used the case against South Carolina's Democrats, calling the lynchers "Scions of Chivalry" and urging the state to hang them.

Accounts differ on the date, with Prosperity briefs giving the 10th, the day the body was found, and the Legette letter giving the 4th; they also differ on her name and age, from Judy Metts, about thirty-five, to “Eliza Cowan, alias Judith Metts,” an “old” woman. The Abbeville Press and Banner alone said the lynching took place "in broad day light"; the local accounts place it after nightfall.

reader.title: Lynching of Judy Metts
bases: A Black woman under arrest for barn-burning was taken from a constable by disguised mounted men and found hanged the next morning (A5, A8, A14).

Judy Metts was taken from a constable by a party of disguised horsemen, later put at twenty-five to thirty men, and hanged to a tree over an accusation of arson (A8, A14, A33, A35); the coroner's jury found she died by hanging at the hands of persons unknown (A8).

The Newberry Herald's local account, the News and Courier dispatch and the Richmond Dispatch telegram agree on the arrest, seizure and hanging, and the governor's reward confirms it (A5, A8, A14, A32).
